final_text: Since Apache Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026), share groups ('Kafka Queues', KIP-932) are production-ready. Several consumers in a share group can read the same partition with per-record acknowledgement, so the number of consumers can exceed the number of partitions.
note: KIP-932 (opened): 'The number of consumers in a share group can exceed the number of partitions in a topic'; 'Records are acknowledged on an individual basis'. Kafka 4.2.0 announcement (Feb 17, 2026): Kafka Queues (Share Groups) 'is now production-ready'. Still true in Kafka 4.3.1 (June 2026, current).

final_text: AWS offers this fan-out pattern as managed services: publish once to an SNS topic and SNS pushes a copy to every subscribed SQS queue, where workers poll and process at their own pace.
note: AWS SNS docs (opened): 'you can publish a message to the topic and Amazon SNS sends an Amazon SQS message to the subscribed queue'; SQS uses 'a polling model'.

final_text: Browsers identify images from their first bytes using the WHATWG MIME Sniffing rules, which recognise ICO, BMP, GIF, WebP, PNG and JPEG signatures. SVG is not sniffed: it must be served with Content-Type image/svg+xml.
note: WHATWG MIME Sniffing 6.1 (opened): image patterns for ICO, BMP, GIF87a/89a, WebP, PNG, JPEG; no SVG pattern. 8.2: 'If the supplied MIME type is an XML MIME type, the computed MIME type is the supplied MIME type', so SVG relies on the served type.

final_text: Examples of format signatures: PNG always starts with the 8 bytes 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A, JPEG with FF D8 FF, BMP with the ASCII letters 'BM', and GIF with 'GIF87a' or 'GIF89a'.
note: PNG spec 5.2 (opened): first eight bytes 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A. MIME Sniffing table: JPEG FF D8 FF, BMP 42 4D ('BM'), GIF87a/GIF89a.

final_text: A static-file handler must not let the URL path escape the static folder (e.g. /static/../../etc/passwd). Werkzeug's send_from_directory, used by Flask, applies safe_join to 'Safely join zero or more untrusted path components to a trusted base directory to avoid escaping the base directory.'
note: Werkzeug utils (opened): safe_join quote is verbatim; send_from_directory 'Uses safe_join() to ensure the path coming from the client is not maliciously crafted to point outside the specified directory.'

final_text: When your own handler returns file bytes, set the Content-Type header yourself (for example from a type stored with the file). MDN warns that browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension, so servers must send the correct type; nginx does this for static files by mapping file extensions to MIME types.
note: MDN MIME types (opened): 'Browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension ... it's important that web servers send the correct MIME type in the response's Content-Type header.' nginx core module (opened): types 'Maps file name extensions to MIME types of responses.' The S3 parenthetical was not backed by an opened source; removed.

final_text: Django serves static files itself only in development (runserver with DEBUG=True); its docs say this method is 'grossly inefficient and probably insecure, so it is unsuitable for production'. In production a web server, a CDN or WhiteNoise serves them.
note: Django docs (opened; Django 6.1): runserver serves static files when DEBUG is True; 'This method is grossly inefficient and probably insecure, so it is unsuitable for production.' Quote verbatim.

final_text: GitHub's 2021 engineering post reports that generating one image takes 280 ms on average, the service produces around two million 'unique-ish' images per day, and 40% of requests are served a cached image.
note: GitHub blog (opened; June 22, 2021): 'Generating an image takes 280ms on average'; about two million 'unique-ish' images a day; about 40% of requests served a cached image. Historical (2021) figures.

final_text: GitHub's generator is 'a little Node.js app' that fetches data through the GitHub GraphQL API, fills an HTML template and captures it with Puppeteer. Rendering HTML in a headless browser is an alternative to drawing with an image library.
note: GitHub blog (opened): 'a little Node.js app' using the GitHub GraphQL API, an HTML template and Puppeteer screenshot.

final_text: Pillow, the maintained fork of PIL, has its own C imaging core and links libraries such as libjpeg, zlib, libtiff and FreeType. To drive ImageMagick from Python you use a separate binding such as Wand.
note: Pillow docs (opened, 12.3.0): 'the friendly PIL fork'; build-from-source page lists libjpeg, zlib, libtiff, libfreetype, libwebp etc. and never mentions ImageMagick. Wand docs: 'a ctypes-based simple ImageMagick binding for Python'.

final_text: The CDN's TTL is usually set by the origin's Cache-Control header: s-maxage sets freshness for shared caches such as CDNs and overrides max-age there, so a card can stay a day at the CDN without browsers caching it as long.
note: MDN Cache-Control (opened): s-maxage 'is ignored by private caches, and overrides the value specified by the max-age directive or the Expires header for shared caches'.

final_text: Open Graph requires four properties on every page: og:title, og:type, og:image and og:url. og:image is 'An image URL which should represent your object within the graph.'
note: ogp.me (opened): required og:title, og:type, og:image, og:url; og:image quote verbatim.

final_text: Gravatar's docs (checked October 2026) say to trim leading and trailing whitespace from the email, lowercase it, and hash it with SHA-256. Skipping the trim or lowercase step gives a different hash, so the avatar is not found.
note: Gravatar hash docs (opened 2026-10-13): 'Trim leading and trailing whitespace', 'Force all characters to lower-case', 'hash the final string with SHA256'. No MD5 mention.

final_text: The avatar URL accepts parameters: s= sets the size (1 to 2048 px, default 80), and d= picks what to show when no avatar exists (a built-in default, your own image URL, or d=404 to get an HTTP 404).
note: Gravatar image docs (opened): https://gravatar.com/avatar/HASH; sizes 1px to 2048px, default 80x80; d=404 returns 'an HTTP 404 (File Not Found) response'; custom URL default allowed.

final_text: Because Gravatar hashes are unsalted and fast, anyone can hash a list of candidate emails and match them against Gravatar URLs, so guessable addresses can be identified. Solar Designer notes that switching from MD5 to SHA-256 is 'almost no change' for this.
note: oss-sec post by Solar Designer (opened; Sep 25, 2024): 'For practical purposes, this sounds like almost no change to me'; Gravatar URLs 'by design allow for quick checking of email addresses against them'; MD5 and SHA-256 'are very fast'.

final_text: PostgreSQL can index an expression, e.g. CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)); a query with WHERE lower(email) = 'x' then searches as fast as any simple index lookup. The cost is that the expression is computed on every insert and on every non-HOT update.
note: PostgreSQL 18.6 docs (opened): lower(col1) example; 'the speed of the search is equivalent to any other simple index query'; cost: expressions 'must be computed for each row insertion and non-HOT update' - 'most updates' replaced by the exact wording.

final_text: MySQL 8 supports functional key parts, e.g. CREATE INDEX idx1 ON t1 ((col1 + col2)). To use such an index the query must contain the same expression; the manual's example shows an index on SUBSTRING(col1, 1, 10) is not used for SUBSTRING(col1, 1, 9).
note: MySQL 8.4 CREATE INDEX (opened): example is CREATE INDEX idx1 ON t1 ((col1 + col2)). The page states the same-expression rule only through its SUBSTRING example ('the WHERE clause must contain SUBSTRING() with the same arguments'); text adjusted to say that.

final_text: In PostgreSQL's default Read Committed level, an UPDATE finds its target rows using a snapshot taken at the start of the statement. Two concurrent mark-active transactions can each clear only the old active row and then activate different photos, leaving two active. Lock the user's row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or keep a single active_photo_id on users.
note: PostgreSQL transaction isolation (opened): Read Committed is the default; UPDATE 'will only find target rows that were committed as of the command start time', then re-evaluates WHERE on the updated row version. I re-derived the scenario: with '... AND is_active = true', T2 skips the old row (now false) and never sees T1's new active row, so both photos end up active.

final_text: The MySQL manual warns that a regular SELECT in a transaction 'does not give enough protection': other transactions can update or delete the rows you just read. Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (or FOR SHARE) so the checked row stays locked until COMMIT.
note: MySQL 8.4 locking reads (opened): 'the regular SELECT statement does not give enough protection'; FOR SHARE/FOR UPDATE locks released at commit or rollback.

final_text: An UPDATE that matches no rows is not an error. In MySQL, ROW_COUNT() after an UPDATE returns the number of rows actually changed (rows matched if the client sets CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS), so the application can check it and issue ROLLBACK when it is 0. Note that an UPDATE that sets a row to the value it already has counts as 0 changed by default.
note: MySQL 8.4 information functions (opened): for UPDATE 'the affected-rows value by default is the number of rows actually changed'; with CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS it is rows matched. Important nuance for this design: re-marking an already-active photo changes 0 rows, so checking for 0 would roll back a harmless request; added.

final_text: The step-by-step narrowing needs an index on photos.user_id. MySQL InnoDB creates an index on a foreign-key column automatically if none exists; PostgreSQL does not, and its docs say indexing the referencing column is often a good idea.
note: MySQL 8.4 FK docs (opened): an index on the referencing columns 'is created on the referencing table automatically if it does not exist'. PostgreSQL docs (opened): 'it is often a good idea to index the referencing columns too ... the declaration of a foreign key constraint does not automatically create an index on the referencing columns.'

final_text: MySQL converts a LEFT JOIN into an inner join when the WHERE condition is null-rejected (it can never be true for a NULL-filled row), as with photos.is_active = true. The rewrite frees the optimizer to pick a better join order.
note: MySQL 8.4 outer join simplification (opened): outer join replaced by inner join when the WHERE condition is null-rejected; definition and the join-order benefit match. Useful but an optimizer detail for most readers.

final_text: CloudFront Origin Access Control lets the CDN read a private S3 bucket by signing its requests. The bucket policy allows only that distribution, so viewers cannot use S3 URLs directly.
note: CloudFront OAC docs (opened): OAC sends authenticated (signed) requests to an S3 origin; bucket policy with AWS:SourceArn condition limits access to that distribution; the OAI section says viewers 'can't use Amazon S3 URLs to access your files outside of CloudFront'.

final_text: A plain CNAME can't sit at the zone apex (gravatar.com): RFC 1034 says no other data may exist at a CNAME's node, and the apex always has SOA and NS records. Using the root domain as a CDN hostname needs provider support such as Cloudflare's CNAME flattening, which answers with the target's IP addresses instead.
note: Cloudflare CNAME flattening (opened): lets you 'Resolve CNAME records at the zone apex to comply with DNS standards'; 'Cloudflare then returns the final IP address instead of a CNAME record.' The page does not itself state the RFC rule, so I added RFC 1034 3.6.2 (opened): 'If a CNAME RR is present at a node, no other data should be present' (the apex always holds SOA and NS records).

final_text: CDN invalidation clears only the CDN's edge caches: a browser or corporate proxy can keep showing the old file until its own copy expires. CloudFront recommends versioned file names for frequently updated files, and invalidations can cost money while versioning does not.
note: CloudFront invalidation docs (opened): recommends versioning for frequently updated files; with invalidation 'the user might continue to see the old version until it expires from those caches' (local or corporate proxy); 'you don't have to pay for invalidating files' with versioning.

final_text: Cloudflare's docs recommend single-file purge (by URL) as the main purge method. It is available on every plan, with rate limits (e.g. 800 URLs per second on Free).
note: Cloudflare purge docs (opened): single-file purge (purge by URL) is 'the recommended method', available on all plans; Free plan up to 800 URLs per second.

final_text: Pillow, the maintained fork of PIL, has its own resize API (Image.resize). ImageMagick is used from Python through the separate Wand package, a ctypes-based binding that requires the MagickWand library.
note: Pillow docs (opened): Image.resize 'Returns a resized copy of this image' (reference page, which I added). Wand docs: 'ctypes-based simple ImageMagick binding', 'it requires MagickWand library'. Largely duplicates A-ID-10, hence optional.

final_text: Cloudflare Images transforms images on the fly from URL parameters (resize, crop, convert to WebP or AVIF), so you don't have to pre-generate variants.
note: Cloudflare image-optimization page (opened): Images 'transforms images on-the-fly via URL parameters'; resizing, cropping, WebP/AVIF conversion. The quoted phrase 'no pre-generated variants needed' is not verbatim on the page; quotes removed.

final_text: Cloudflare's engineering blog (2021) says 'We developed Image Resizing in Rust', with its own image processing and compression libraries, so the teacher's half-remembered ImageMagick-based blog is unlikely to describe Cloudflare's current product.
note: Cloudflare blog (opened; published Sep 15, 2021): 'We developed Image Resizing in Rust'; processing and compression parts packaged as Rust libraries. The post never mentions ImageMagick, so 'rather than built on ImageMagick' is the checker's inference; softened.

final_text: In MySQL, BOOL is a synonym for TINYINT(1); the (1) is only a display width, so the column can actually hold any value from -128 to 127. Add a CHECK constraint if only 0/1 should be allowed.
note: MySQL 8.4 numeric types (opened): BOOL/BOOLEAN 'are synonyms for TINYINT(1)'; signed range -128 to 127; 'Display width is unrelated to the range of values a type can store' (and display width is deprecated).

final_text: PostgreSQL has no TINYINT: its smallest integer type is smallint (2 bytes). A 1-byte state column there is boolean, or use smallint with a CHECK constraint.
note: PostgreSQL 18 numeric types (opened): integers are two-, four- and eight-byte; smallint is 2 bytes, no tinyint. Boolean type page: boolean is 1 byte.

final_text: MySQL starts each connection with autocommit enabled: it commits after every statement that does not return an error. Use START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT to group several statements into one transaction.
note: MySQL 8.4 autocommit page (opened): each new connection has autocommit enabled and commits after each statement that does not return an error; START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT groups statements.

final_text: MongoDB caps a single document at 16 MiB. 10,000 user ids fit well under that, so the practical reasons to move tags to separate entries are the cost of rewriting and reading one ever-growing document and the need to paginate, rather than the hard limit.
note: MongoDB limits (opened): 'The maximum BSON document size is 16 mebibytes.'

final_text: Arrays can be indexed: MongoDB automatically makes an index on an array field a multikey index, with one entry per distinct value, and PostgreSQL indexes arrays with GIN (built-in array_ops supports @>, && and <@). PostgreSQL's docs still advise that if you search for array elements, a separate table with a row per element is easier to search and scales better.
note: MongoDB multikey docs (opened): created automatically on array fields; 'For each distinct value in the array, MongoDB creates a separate entry' - so per distinct value, not per element. PostgreSQL GIN array_ops (opened): &&, @>, <@, =. PostgreSQL arrays tip (opened): 'searching for specific array elements can be a sign of database misdesign ... easier to search, and is likely to scale better'.

final_text: Facebook's Graph API stores photo tag positions exactly this way: a tag's x and y are given 'as a percentage offset from the left edge' and 'from the top edge' of the picture.
note: Facebook Graph API photo tags (opened): x 'as a percentage offset from the left edge of the picture', y 'from the top edge'. The page does not say 'floats'; removed.

final_text: Object-detection datasets use the second form: YOLO labels store each box as class x_center y_center width height, normalized to 0-1 by dividing x and width by the image width and y and height by the image height.
note: Ultralytics detect docs (opened): 'class x_center y_center width height', normalized 0-1 by dividing x and width by image width, y and height by image height.

final_text: On 2 November 2021 Meta shut down the Face Recognition system on Facebook and said it would delete more than a billion face templates; people can no longer turn on face recognition for suggested tagging.
note: Meta newsroom (opened; Nov 2, 2021): 'We're shutting down the Face Recognition system on Facebook'; 'delete more than a billion people's individual facial recognition templates'; 'People will no longer be able to turn on face recognition for suggested tagging'.

final_text: In role-based access control (NIST), users are assigned roles and each role carries permissions. A 'who can tag me' setting is a per-user access rule about other users, closer to an access control list; Google's Zanzibar is a global system for storing and evaluating such ACLs for services including Drive, Photos and YouTube.
note: NIST RBAC page (opened): 'Each user is assigned one or more roles' and 'each role is assigned one or more privileges'. Zanzibar abstract (opened): 'a global system for storing and evaluating access control lists' serving 'Calendar, Cloud, Drive, Maps, Photos, and YouTube'. The abstract does not describe user-to-user relationship modelling; wording narrowed to what it says.

final_text: Amazon's Builders' Library argues against most fallbacks: fallback code is hard to test, often has latent bugs and can make outages worse. It prefers making the primary path more robust, letting callers retry, and, if a fallback is kept, running it continuously so it is always exercised.
note: AWS Builders' Library (opened): 'fallback logic is hard to test'; fallbacks have 'latent bugs'; they 'often make the outage worse'. Its alternatives are making the primary more robust, letting callers retry, pushing data ahead of time, and running both paths continuously. 'Failing fast' is not one of its named alternatives; replaced.

final_text: Android supports clubbing notifications: related notifications can be put in one group with a summary (Android 7.0+), and the system may group an app's notifications automatically once it posts four or more. Android's docs also suggest updating an existing notification instead of posting new ones.
note: Android notification groups (opened): groups with a required summary from Android 7.0 (API 24); if an app posts four or more notifications without a group, 'the system may group them automatically' (device-dependent) - 'auto-groups' overstated; also suggests updating an existing notification.

final_text: PostgreSQL states the rule behind this choice: equality conditions on leading index columns plus an inequality on the first column without an equality limit the part of the index scanned. With to = ? AND ts > ?, an index on (to, ts, ...) reads only the recent entries; (to, from, ts) reads all of the recipient's entries.
note: PostgreSQL multicolumn indexes (opened): 'equality constraints on leading columns, plus any inequality constraints on the first column that does not have an equality constraint, will always be used to limit the portion of the index that is scanned.' MySQL 8.4 leftmost-prefix rule (opened) consistent.

final_text: In SQL the aggregate is COUNT(DISTINCT expr), which counts distinct non-NULL values. FROM and TO are reserved words in MySQL, so columns named that way must be quoted with backticks; names like sender_id/recipient_id avoid the problem.
note: MySQL 8.4 aggregate functions (opened): COUNT(DISTINCT expr) 'Returns a count of the number of rows with different non-NULL expr values.' Keywords page: FROM (R), TO (R); reserved words need quoting (backticks).

final_text: In Redis, SCARD returns the number of members of a set in O(1), and returns 0 if the key does not exist, so a cleared badge needs no special case.
note: Redis SCARD (opened): complexity O(1); returns the cardinality 'or 0 if the key does not exist'.

final_text: Redis SADD ignores members already in the set and returns how many new members were added, 0 for a repeat sender. So the write is idempotent, and the worker can tell whether the sender was new.
note: Redis SADD (opened): 'Specified members that are already a member of this set are ignored'; returns 'the number of elements that were added to the set, not including all the elements already present'.

final_text: Redis DEL on a set is O(M) in the number of members (O(1) only for string values). UNLINK removes the key in O(1) and reclaims memory in a background thread. For small per-user sets either is cheap.
note: Redis DEL (opened): non-string key is 'O(M) where M is the number of elements'; string O(1). UNLINK: 'O(1) for each key removed regardless of its size', memory reclaimed 'in a different thread'.

final_text: Redis can do the auxiliary 'check and set' in one atomic command: SET key value NX sets the key only if it does not exist and returns OK when it did (nil otherwise). Adding EX seconds gives the key a TTL, so stale entries eventually disappear.
note: Redis SET (opened): NX 'Only set the key if it does not already exist'; EX seconds; reply OK when set, null when NX and the key exists.

final_text: An alternative to one key per (receiver, sender) pair is one hash per receiver: HSETNX B C 1 sets field C only if it is absent and returns 1 if it did. A single DEL B clears the user, and since Redis 7.4 HEXPIRE can give individual fields a TTL.
note: Redis HSETNX (opened): sets field only if it does not yet exist; returns 1 if set, 0 otherwise. HEXPIRE (opened): field TTLs, since 7.4.0.

final_text: In a Redis Cluster, keys are spread across hash slots, so B_C and B_D can land on different nodes. A hash tag such as {B}_C and {B}_D hashes only the part in braces, so all of a user's keys share one slot and can be handled together.
note: Redis cluster spec (opened): 16384 hash slots; 'If the key contains a "{...}" pattern only the substring between { and } is hashed'; hash tags put keys in the same slot.

final_text: Kafka writes events with the same key to the same partition, and a consumer reads a partition's events in the order they were written. Keying on-message-unsent events by recipient id therefore sends all of a recipient's events to one worker, which can collapse them before writing.
note: Kafka intro (opened): 'Events with the same event key (e.g., a customer or vehicle ID) are written to the same partition'; consumers 'always read that partition's events in exactly the same order as they were written'.

final_text: Batched Redis writes can be sent with pipelining: many commands go out without waiting for each reply. That saves round trips and system calls, and Redis reports throughput rising up to about 10x the unpipelined baseline.
note: Redis pipelining (opened): send multiple commands without waiting for replies; many commands read with a single read() and replies with a single write(); throughput 'eventually reaches 10 times the baseline'.

final_text: A WebSocket connection can look open after the client has gone (e.g. lost network). RFC 6455 Ping/Pong frames are the protocol's way to check: a Ping 'may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive', and the peer must answer with a Pong.
note: RFC 6455 5.5.2 (opened): quote verbatim (a non-normative NOTE); 'Upon receipt of a Ping frame, an endpoint MUST send a Pong frame in response, unless it already received a Close frame.'

final_text: Redis replication is asynchronous and is documented as usable 'for scalability, to have multiple replicas for read-only queries'. In Redis Cluster, clients send READONLY to read from replicas where possibly stale data is acceptable.
note: Redis replication (opened): 'Redis uses asynchronous replication'; 'Replication can be used both for scalability, to have multiple replicas for read-only queries'. Cluster spec: clients 'can use replicas in order to scale reads using the READONLY command'.

final_text: In MySQL, plain EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's plan (how it would process the statement), while EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the statement and reports real timings. On a production console, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE with care: heavy queries really execute, and data-changing statements really change data.
note: MySQL 8.4 EXPLAIN (opened): EXPLAIN ANALYZE 'runs a statement and produces EXPLAIN output along with timing'; plain EXPLAIN shows 'how it would process the statement' (the page does not literally say it does not run). Wording aligned; added that EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a data-changing statement changes data.

final_text: MongoDB gives set semantics on an array field: $addToSet adds a value only if it is not already present. Updates to a single document are atomic, so concurrent workers adding senders for the same user don't corrupt the set.
note: MongoDB $addToSet (opened): 'adds a value to an array unless the value is already present'. Atomicity page (opened): a write is atomic at the level of a single document.
